revisions.draft:
Many students at our school want a community garden. Our school should start one because it would give students fresh food and teach responsibility.

In the synthetic class survey, 62% of students said they would try vegetables from a school garden. This result shows that some students are interested in fresh food. Students could take home tomatoes and lettuce.

A garden also teaches responsibility. Students would water plants and pull weeds. They would learn that living things need care. When students care for plants without being reminded, they practice noticing shared responsibilities. This can help them contribute to their school community.

In conclusion, our school should build a community garden.

scenarios.name: Long grade-7 informational essay with source
scenarios.draft:
School gardens are often described as outdoor classrooms because they connect scientific ideas with daily activity. A garden gives students a place to observe plant growth, but the educational value depends on what students actually do and record. A patch of soil by itself does not explain a process.

Plant growth begins with conditions that support seeds. Water enters a seed and activates processes that allow a root and shoot to emerge. Soil, light, and temperature influence whether the young plant continues to grow. Students can observe these changes by measuring the same plants on regular days. A notebook with dates and measurements is more useful than a general statement that the plants are doing fine.

Pollination is another process that students can study. Bees and other animals may carry pollen between flowers. This movement can help plants form seeds and fruit. Students who only write that bees are nice miss the relationship between the insect and the plant. A better observation records where the bee lands, what it does, and what part of the plant changes later.

A garden also supports lessons about evidence. If one plant grows taller than another, students should compare light, water, soil, and plant type before offering an explanation. The tallest plant did not necessarily receive the best care. A single observation cannot show every cause, and a class should avoid turning one result into a rule for every garden.

Organization matters during these investigations. Students can divide responsibilities for watering, measuring, and recording, but they should use the same procedure each time. If one group changes the schedule while another group does not, the records may be difficult to compare. Shared directions help students understand whether differences came from the plants or from the investigation.

Teachers can connect the garden to writing by asking students to explain one process using their observations. The strongest explanation should include a central idea, relevant details, and a clear sequence. Students should identify which claims came from the supplied passage, which came from observation, and which remain uncertain. They should also avoid listing every measurement without explaining why it matters.

A school garden therefore works best as a repeated investigation rather than a one-time decoration. Students can return to the same plants, compare new evidence with earlier notes, and revise their explanations when the evidence changes. This process makes the garden useful for both science and informational writing because it rewards careful observation, organized records, and bounded conclusions.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Explain how a school garden can support scientific observation and evidence-based informational writing.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Use the supplied passage, organize by subtopic, and prioritize explanation rather than listing facts.
scenarios.source_material:
Paragraph 1: Seeds take in water before a root and shoot emerge. Light, temperature, water, and soil conditions affect later growth. Regular measurements taken under consistent conditions are more comparable than occasional observations.

Paragraph 2: Pollinators can carry pollen between flowers. This transfer can help plants form seeds and fruit. Observing where an insect lands and what it does can help students describe the process, but one observation does not establish every cause of plant growth.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: A small prioritized issue set and accurate references across multiple paragraphs

scenarios.name: Grade-6 argument with non-obscuring language errors
scenarios.draft:
Our school should start a garden because it can teach responsibility and give students a useful reason to observe plants. In a synthetic class survey, 31 of 50 students said they would try vegetables from a garden. This detail shows interest in using the garden, although it does not prove that every student would participate.

The garden would also give a students regular jobs. Students learns to notice when plants need water and to complete a task in weekend without being reminded. These actions can build habits that matter in other shared spaces. The evidence about interest supports the plan, while the daily jobs explain how the plan could help students over time.

Some people may worry that gardening takes time away from class. A teacher can connect the jobs to science observations, so the activity has a clear learning purpose. Students could still make mistake in a notebook, but the mistake would give them something to investigate. The garden is worth trying because it combines student interest, shared responsibility, and a realistic way to study plants.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Write a source-based argument about whether the school should start a garden.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Prioritize claim, evidence, reasoning, and organization. Language corrections are optional unless they obscure meaning.
scenarios.source_material: Paragraph 1: A synthetic class survey included 50 students. 31 said they would try vegetables from a school garden. The survey measured interest and did not measure participation or health outcomes.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Prioritize thinking and organization over non-obscuring article, tense, and preposition errors

scenarios.name: Strong outer paragraphs and weak middle explanation
scenarios.draft:
Our school should create a student library committee because students can help choose books that match their interests and reading goals. A committee would give readers a structured way to recommend titles, explain gaps in the collection, and discuss choices with the librarian. This approach would support student voice without asking students to make purchasing decisions alone.

Students have many interests. Some like mysteries and others like science. The committee would meet every week.

Reading is important for learning. Books can be about different places. Students would enjoy the meetings.

For these reasons, a student library committee would give readers a meaningful role in improving the collection while preserving the librarian's professional judgment. The school could begin with a small trial, review student recommendations, and decide whether the process helps readers find more engaging books.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Argue whether the school should create a student library committee.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Keep the strong introduction and conclusion. Develop the middle paragraphs with specific reasons and connections.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Target middle paragraphs for explanation and cohesion without forcing changes to strong sections

scenarios.name: Grade-7 informational register shifts
scenarios.draft:
Photosynthesis is kinda amazing because plants make their own food. The aforementioned botanical mechanism utilizes luminous energy to facilitate carbohydrate synthesis. Leaves take in sunlight and use it to change water and carbon dioxide into sugar. This process is super cool and helps plants grow.

Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy. The stomata, those tiny little things under the leaf, allow carbon dioxide to enter. Oxygen is released during the process. People often think plants get food from soil, but soil mainly provides water and minerals rather than sugar. Understanding this difference helps readers see why light and air matter so much to plant growth.
scenarios.assignment_prompt: Explain photosynthesis to another seventh-grade student.
scenarios.teacher_directions: Use a consistent explanatory register. Casual or formal wording is not automatically wrong; consider the audience and purpose.
scenarios.acceptance_focus: Optional register-consistency focus without declaring either phrasing inherently wrong
